reflection_text.6:
The mathematical structure for an all-or-nothing vaccine with completely protected proportion p and 1-p biologically unvaccinated is unchanged:

S0(t)=exp[-∫λ0], Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
hv(t)=λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
HR(t)=hv/λ0=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0], HR(0)=1-p, HR(t) monotone decreasing to 0.

Cumulative incidence ratio [1-Sv]/[1-S0]=1-p is constant, so 1-RRcum=p is the proportion protected.

Finite follow-up incidence density ratio is a time average of HR(t).
With N0 per arm Events_v=N0(1-p)[1-S0(T)], PT_v=N0∫0^T[p+(1-p)S0]dt,
Events_u=N0[1-S0(T)], PT_u=N0∫0^T S0 dt

IRR(T)=(1-p)∫0^T S0 /[pT+(1-p)∫0^T S0] < HR(0)=1-p for T>0, λ0>0
With constant λ0: IRR(T)=(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[λ0pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]]<1-p
1-IRR(T)=λ0pT/[λ0pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]]>p →1 as T→∞.

Thus the marginal rate-based 1-IRR is inflated relative to the initial instantaneous population average hazard reduction p and increases with follow-up. The pT risk-free person-time dilutes the vaccinated denominator.

Definitional split persists in round 3.

Population-average per-exposure view: with constant exposure rate e and per-exposure infection probability π, IR0=eπ, IRv=e[p·0+(1-p)π]=(1-p)IR0. Hence IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p, and average per-exposure risk π̄v=(1-p)π. Under rare disease / S0≈1 / T→0 this is identified as the population average per-exposure VE. Colleagues 1,5,7,12 in round 3 argue this is the conventional epidemiologic definition: the time-varying h_v(t) is the hazard conditional on remaining under observation, declining because the 1-p susceptible fraction is selectively removed while the p protected fraction contributes zero-event person-time. That is a depletion-of-susceptibles composition/selection effect, not a change in per-contact infection probability for an individual who remains susceptible. The marginal rate already integrates over protected person-time, giving a constant population rate ratio 1-p under constant exposure. They answer C correctly estimate.

Instantaneous per-exposure/biological view: biological per-exposure efficacy is the initial instantaneous reduction 1-HR(0)=p for the susceptible pool. Because HR(t) falls, the time-averaged IRR(T)<1-p, hence 1-IRR(T)>p. The protected person-time pT inflates rate-based VE. Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,10,11 in round 3 answer A overestimate. They note equality 1-IRR=p is recovered only in the rare-disease/S0≈1/T→0 Poisson idealisation where depletion is masked; on the usual instantaneous/biological per-exposure definition the finite follow-up marginal rate ratio is a time-averaged overestimate, the cumulative risk ratio being the quantity that stays at p.

Changes in positions: Colleague 1 now C, Colleague 12 now C, Colleague 7 now C, consistent with population-average view. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 hold A overestimate, with Colleague 10,11 explicitly noting the rare-disease limit recovers the population average.

Unresolved: whether “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” means the population average reduction in risk per exposure under constant exposure, which coincides with 1-IRR in the Poisson rare-disease idealisation, or the instantaneous biological per-exposure reduction HR(0)=1-p. The mathematical depletion result HR(t)<1-p and IRR(T)<1-p for any non-trivial follow-up suggests the conventional rate-based 1-IRR overstates the initial instantaneous per-exposure efficacy, with equality only under rare disease/T→0. The cumulative risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at p for an all-or-nothing vaccine.

3.text:
A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing mechanism with proportion completely protected p

$S_{v}(t)=p+(1-p)S_{0}(t),\qquad S_{0}(t)=\exp[-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{0}]$

$h_{v}(t)=-\dot S_{v}/S_{v}= \lambda_{0}(t)\frac{(1-p)S_{0}(t)}{p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)}$

$HR(t)=\frac{h_{v}(t)}{\lambda_{0}(t)}=\frac{(1-p)S_{0}(t)}{p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)}$

$HR(0)=1-p,\quad HR'(t)<0,\quad HR(t)\to0$.

The instantaneous biological per-exposure reduction in the still susceptible pool is
$VE_{pe}(0)=1-HR(0)=p$ and the cumulative risk ratio is constant

$\frac{1-S_{v}(T)}{1-S_{0}(T)}=1-p,\qquad 1-RR=p$.

The incidence density that is reported is events / total person-time, i.e. a time average of $HR(t)$. With $N_{0}$ per arm

$Events_{v}=N_{0}(1-p)[1-S_{0}(T)],\; PT_{v}=N_{0}\int_{0}^{T}\!\big[p+(1-p)S_{0}(t)\big]dt$
$Events_{u}=N_{0}[1-S_{0}(T)],\; PT_{u}=N_{0}\int_{0}^{T}\!S_{0}(t)dt$

$IRR(T)=\frac{(1-p)\int_{0}^{T}S_{0}(t)dt}{pT+(1-p)\int_{0}^{T}S_{0}(t)dt}<HR(0)=1-p$
for any $T>0,\;\lambda_{0}>0$.

With constant $\lambda_{0}$

$IRR(T)=\frac{(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}{\lambda_{0}pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}<1-p$

$1-IRR(T)=\frac{\lambda_{0}pT}{\lambda_{0}pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_{0}T}]}>p\to1$ as $T\to\infty$.

The $pT$ completely protected person-time is added to the vaccinated denominator with zero events while events accrue only in the $1-p$ susceptible fraction which is selectively depleted by infection. The marginal hazard ratio therefore falls with time and the person-time averaged $IRR$ is $<HR(0)$. Hence

$1-IRR(T)>1-HR(0)=p$,

i.e. the naïve $1$-incidence rate ratio is inflated relative to the initial instantaneous per-exposure efficacy $p$. The bias grows with follow-up and cumulative incidence.

Equality $1-IRR=p$ is recovered only in the rare-disease $S_{0}\approx1$, $\int S_{0}\approx T$, $T\to0$ Poisson idealisation where depletion of susceptibles is masked. On the usual instantaneous/biological per-exposure definition $VE_{pe}(0)=p$ the finite-follow-up marginal rate ratio is a time-averaged overestimate; the cumulative risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at $p$ for an all-or-nothing vaccine. This is the classic depletion-of-susceptibles / protected person-time bias for all-or-nothing vs leaky mechanisms.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

The disagreement here is mostly definitional, and it helps to be explicit about which definition of “per-exposure” is being used in trial practice.

With a constant exposure rate e and a per-exposure infection probability π in a fully susceptible host, IR0 = e π. For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p is made hazard zero and a fraction 1-p is biologically unvaccinated. On a cohort average the marginal force of infection is the mixture

IRv = p·0 + (1-p) e π = (1-p) IR0

so that IRR = IRv/IR0 = 1-p and 1-IRR = p. The average per-exposure risk in the vaccinated cohort is π̄v = p·0 + (1-p)π = (1-p)π, hence π̄v/π = 1-p = IRR and the population-average per-exposure efficacy VEpe = 1 - π̄v/π = p = 1-IRR. That is the quantity a Poisson incidence density ratio is designed to recover.

The expression

h_v(t)=λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],   HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0]

is the marginal hazard conditional on remaining in the risk set. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is selectively removed by infection while the p protected fraction stays in the denominator contributing zero-event person-time. That is depletion of susceptibles / composition selection on who remains at risk, not a change in the per-contact infection probability for an individual who remains susceptible. For a still-susceptible vaccinee the per-exposure risk stays π, zero for a protected vaccinee.

The marginal incidence rate that enters a rate ratio already integrates over protected person-time p t and susceptible person-time (1-p)∫S0. With constant exposure that integration gives a constant population rate ratio 1-p. The time dependence is a property of the conditional hazard HR(t) and of the cumulative incidence risk ratio on the survival scale, not of the marginal incidence density ratio.

In the rare-disease / steady-state Poisson conditions under which vaccine trials are run, S0(t)≈1 and ∫S0≈T, so the conditional variation is masked and the marginal rate ratio coincides with the population-average per-exposure reduction. Colleague 10 himself notes “IRv=(1-p)IR0, 1-IRR=p is recovered only in the rare-disease / S0≈1 / T→0 Poisson idealisation” and describes an overestimation only on an instantaneous/biological per-exposure definition at t=0.

With the usual epidemiologic definition of per-exposure VE as the population average reduction in risk per exposure under constant exposure, 1-IRR recovers p, the proportion completely protected, for an all-or-nothing mechanism. The bias people describe is a bias of the cumulative risk ratio and of the instantaneous conditional hazard, not a bias of the incidence density ratio.

C. correctly estimate

The disagreement here is mostly definitional, and it helps to be explicit about which definition of “per-exposure” is being used in trial practice.

With a constant exposure rate e and a per-exposure infection probability π in a fully susceptible host, IR0 = e π. For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p is made hazard zero and a fraction 1-p is biologically unvaccinated. On a cohort average the marginal force of infection is the mixture

IRv = p·0 + (1-p) e π = (1-p) IR0

so that IRR = IRv/IR0 = 1-p and 1-IRR = p. The average per-exposure risk in the vaccinated cohort is π̄v = p·0 + (1-p)π = (1-p)π, hence π̄v/π = 1-p = IRR and the population-average per-exposure efficacy VEpe = 1 - π̄v/π = p = 1-IRR. That is the quantity a Poisson incidence density ratio is designed to recover.

The expression

h_v(t)=λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],   HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0]

is the marginal hazard conditional on remaining in the risk set. It declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is selectively removed by infection while the p protected fraction stays in the denominator contributing zero-event person-time. That is depletion of susceptibles / composition selection on who remains at risk, not a change in the per-contact infection probability for an individual who remains susceptible. For a still-susceptible vaccinee the per-exposure risk stays π, zero for a protected vaccinee.

The marginal incidence rate that enters a rate ratio already integrates over protected person-time p t and susceptible person-time (1-p)∫S0. With constant exposure that integration gives a constant population rate ratio 1-p. The time dependence is a property of the conditional hazard HR(t) and of the cumulative incidence risk ratio on the survival scale, not of the marginal incidence density ratio.

In the rare-disease / steady-state Poisson conditions under which vaccine trials are run, S0(t)≈1 and ∫S0≈T, so the conditional variation is masked and the marginal rate ratio coincides with the population-average per-exposure reduction. Colleague 10 himself notes “IRv=(1-p)IR0, 1-IRR=p is recovered only in the rare-disease / S0≈1 / T→0 Poisson idealisation” and describes an overestimation only on an instantaneous/biological per-exposure definition at t=0.

With the usual epidemiologic definition of per-exposure VE as the population average reduction in risk per exposure under constant exposure, 1-IRR recovers p, the proportion completely protected, for an all-or-nothing mechanism. The bias people describe is a bias of the cumulative risk ratio and of the instantaneous conditional hazard, not a bias of the incidence density ratio.

reflection_text.4:
The mechanistic picture is stable and is the common reference.

All-or-nothing with fraction p completely immune, 1-p identical to unvaccinated, baseline hazard λ0, S0=exp[-∫λ0].
Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
hv(t)=λ0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
HR(t)=hv/λ0=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)], HR(0)=1-p, monotone ↓ to 0.
Cumulative risk ratio is constant: [1-Sv(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p → 1-RR=p.

Marginal incidence density over 0,T is a time average of HR(t). With constant λ0
IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]/[λ p T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] <1-p
1-IRR(T)= λ p T/[λ p T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] >p →1 as T→∞.
The pT risk-free person-time is added to the vaccinated denominator with zero events while events accrue only in the 1-p fraction which is being depleted. The naïve 1-incidence rate ratio is inflated relative to the instantaneous per-exposure reduction at t=0, VEinst(0)=1-HR(0)=p.

Camp A, now 8 colleagues: 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9. Argument: 1-IRR is a person-time average of decreasing HR(t). HR(0)=1-p is the biological instantaneous per-exposure efficacy for the susceptible pool. Because HR(t)<HR(0) for t>0, IRR(T)<1-p and 1-IRR(T)>p, bias grows with follow-up and cumulative incidence. The cumulative risk ratio, not the rate ratio, stays at p for all-or-nothing. Equality 1-IRR=p is recovered only in the rare-disease / S0≈1 / T→0 Poisson idealisation where depletion is masked.

Camp C, now 4 colleagues: 1,12,5,7. Argument: with constant exposure rate e and per-exposure infection prob π, IR0=eπ, IRv=p·0+(1-p)eπ=(1-p)IR0, IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p. Population average per-exposure risk π̄v=(1-p)π → VEpop=p. The time-varying HR(t) is the marginal hazard conditional on remaining under observation: it declines because the 1-p susceptible fraction is selectively removed while the p protected fraction stays in denominator contributing zero-event person-time. That is a depletion-of-susceptibles composition selection effect, not a change in per-contact infection probability for an individual who remains susceptible. Under rare disease/steady state the marginal rate ratio coincides with the population average per-exposure effect.

Definitional conflict remains: instantaneous/biological per-exposure VE =1-HR(0)=p for which 1-IRR is upward biased vs population-average per-exposure VE under constant exposure Poisson, for which 1-IRR is unbiased.

reflection_text.11:
The all-or-nothing model is $S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S_0(t)$, $S_0(t)=\exp[-\int_0^t\lambda_0]$, $h_v(t)=\lambda_0(t)(1-p)S_0(t)/[p+(1-p)S_0(t)]$, $HR(t)=(1-p)S_0(t)/[p+(1-p)S_0(t)]$. $HR(0)=1-p$, $HR'(t)<0$, $HR(t)\to0$. Cumulative risk ratio is constant $[1-S_v]/[1-S_0]=1-p$, so $1-RR=p$ is the proportion completely protected.

Rate-based quantity: events$_v=N_0(1-p)[1-S_0(T)]$, PT$_v=N_0\int_0^T[p+(1-p)S_0]$, events$_u=N_0[1-S_0(T)]$, PT$_u=N_0\int_0^TS_0$. Hence $IRR(T)=\frac{(1-p)\int_0^TS_0}{pT+(1-p)\int_0^TS_0}<HR(0)=1-p$ for $T>0$. With constant $\lambda_0$, $IRR(T)=\frac{(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_0T}]}{\lambda_0pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_0T}]}<1-p$, $1-IRR(T)=\frac{\lambda_0pT}{\lambda_0pT+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda_0T}]}>p\to1$. The $pT$ risk-free person-time inflates the vaccinated denominator while events accrue only in the $1-p$ susceptible fraction which is depleted, so the person-time averaged $HR$ is $<HR(0)$.

Instantaneous/biological camp 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9: true per-exposure reduction for the still susceptible pool is $VE_{pe}(0)=1-HR(0)=p$. The finite-follow-up marginal $1-IRR(T)$ is a time average of a decreasing $HR(t)$ and therefore overstates $p$. Equality $1-IRR=p$ only in rare-disease/Poisson steady state $S_0\approx1$, $\int S_0\approx T$, $T\to0$.

Population-average camp 1,12,5,7: with constant exposure $e$ and per-exposure infection prob $\pi$, $IR_0=e\pi$, $IR_v=p\cdot0+(1-p)e\pi=(1-p)IR_0$, so $IRR=1-p$, $1-IRR=p$. Average per-exposure risk $\bar\pi_v=(1-p)\pi$, so population-average per-exposure $VE=1-\bar\pi_v/\pi=p=1-IRR$. The declining $HR(t)$ is depletion-of-susceptibles composition selection, not a change in per-contact $\pi$ for a still susceptible individual. Under the usual trial $S_0\approx1$ Poisson idealisation the marginal rate ratio coincides with the population average per-exposure reduction.

Current round 4: majority A overestimate 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9; minority C correctly estimate 1,12,5,7. Colleague 1 moved B underestimate → C correctly estimate. No B support this round. Unresolved is the definition of “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” intended: instantaneous biological reduction $1-HR(0)=p$ vs population-average reduction per exposure under constant exposure $p$. Under the instantaneous/biological definition $1-IRR$ overestimates; under the conventional epidemiologic population-average definition $1-IRR$ recovers $p$ in the rare disease / steady-state limit used in practice.
